utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kardum, before we continue, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Then Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you give us any indication as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I could complete my cross-examination within an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the other parties, could they give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Approximately an hour and a half, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that there's a fair chance that somewhere in the middle of the second session, certainly not later than the end of the second session that we could conclude the testimony of the witness. Mr. Margetts, unless you would have hours an hours for re-examination...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then I ask this, also, for the other witness waiting so that we do not keep him unnecessarily. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kardum. Today we shall latch onto where we ended yesterday, and we shall go back to the question of sanitization and civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D348. Can I ask the registry for D348, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, we said that civil protection was the organisation that was in charge of sanitising the terrain upon the end of combat activities. You will now see a document compiled by the chief of the police administration in which you work, Mr. Ivan Cetina, the date being the 8th of August in which the Ministry of the Interior sent to the operational headquarters of the action Return numerical data on mobilised forces of civilian protection. So if we look at page 2, we shall see that there were a total, on the 8th of August, 1995, that is, a total of 157 members of civilian protection mobilised to sanitize the terrain, clear up human corpses; 27 of them to clear up animal carcasses; 24 persons for pyrotechnical -- for clearing mines and explosives, that is. What was the use of the crew for the clearing up of mines and explosives in the sanitization of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I remember the mines and explosives clearance crew had written order and obligation to check for mines and explosives, every corpse and the surroundings of every body or animal carcass and to see whether the area around any such found bodies was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We see that of de-mining of -- of the CSEs, there was 16. You said yesterday that these teams, sanitation teams had to have one forensic technician because there might be the suspicion of a crime having been committed, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then we have general-purpose civilian protection units who were engaged in rounding up livestock. Do you remember, Mr. Kardum, what kind of a uniform members of the civilian protection wore, if any?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, members of the civilian protection had some sort of a blue uniform, something similar to the reserve police force uniforms, if they wore any, that is. If they didn't, they had civilian clothes with some patches on the left sleeve where was some sort of an orange-coloured mark, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. If we were to look at the following page in this document, we would see a list of persons found during the sanitization of the terrain. You can see that, of course, this was a routine procedure in sanitizing the terrain, was it not? Have you encountered documents of this kind?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, except I saw them in a different form, a tabular form, but they reflected more or less this. They contained these columns, serial number, identification number, status, the place of burial, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for your reference, Your Honours, similar documents have been also tendered under Exhibits D351 and 352. They are only -- they only concern different periods but are on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'd like that ask you, Mr. Kardum, something that we already broached yesterday; namely, if when examining the terrain you found a body with obvious signs of violence which would indicate that a crime had been committed, then you would inform the competent police station about it, would you not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The police station would then, through its operative duty service, inform the operative duty -- operations duty service in the Zadar police administration, which was competent over Knin in terms of crime, and then a team would be set up to conduct the onsite investigation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The central police station would, as a rule, inform the operations duty service of the police administration but certainly during the period when the operations headquarters at the level of that police administration was functioning. They would also in parallel inform the criminal police and the investigating magistrate in order to conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the on-site investigation team would comprise the investigating judge, who would be - so to speak - the leader of the on-site investigation to be conducted. The competent prosecutor and the forensic technicians or the crime scene examiners and, as you said, the forensic medicine exert expert or the court pathologist as you said yesterday. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me as a connoisseur of crime forensics that it is only the court expert who was the competent person to competently conclude what kind of injury had been sustained by the body that was the subject of the on-site investigation, and of what nature such wound or injury was or what it listen inflicted by, and that was his basic role, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But I do have to say, also, this, Your Honours, that the police, the regularly uniformed police was under the obligation to provide combat security in these instances because there was always a danger of some remnants of enemy troops in the area being active. And in fact, I saw once a document in which a Chief Cetina instructed the police stations in the area of the PU Knin that they must provide combat security to on-site inspection teams when they attended the scene as well as to civilian protection teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Let us go back to the on-site investigation. So after the on-site investigation has been conducted, minutes or a record is drawn up there on; and if any doubt is established - suspicion, that is - as to the commission of a criminal offence, then the police conducts what is referred to as the preliminary processing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this preliminary processing, certain measures, i.e., informative interviews are conducted; material evidence is possibly collected; and once the processing is finished, the compiled file is submitted to the district attorney to the competent prosecutor for his decision, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, the district attorney, i.e. the prosecutor's office decides whether to institute criminal proceedings, namely conduct an investigation or indict the -- the suspects or not. Namely, this is exclusively within the competence of the prosecutor's office, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In so doing, the police, which conducted the preliminary processing of this file, is -- has no further influence on the further procedure, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the investigating judge who is completely in charge of all further procedures. He can possibly instruct the police to take some further investigating measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, Mr. Kardum, how many court experts, pathologists, and district attorneys and investigating judges were available to cover the territory of the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there were just two pathologists; Dr. Josip Duela [phoen] was one, and Dr. Kevarica [phoen] was the other one. I'm not sure whether there was a third one. I don't think so. Of investigating judge - this the county court in Zadar - 's competence because municipal courts are not in charge of such cases but only county courts [as interpreted]. I believe that there were five or six investigating judges who were also to cover all subject matters and as many, I believe, district attorneys or prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your recollection, what was the average duration of such a procedure from the moment there was a report about the -- being a suspicion about a crime having been committed up to the moment when this entire process conducted by the police and investigating judge reached a court?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. The on-site investigation's duration or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no. What was the total duration of the entire procedure if we add up the on-site investigation, the police processing of the case, the investigation undertaken by the investigating judge up to the moment when perhaps an indictment would be filed before the competent Court. How much time would relapse between the beginning of this process until the file appeared before the Court?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the particular case. Some of the cases are still going on, and work is still in progress in respect of them. Where we file the complaints, criminal complaints against unknown perpetrators, we still have some of those cases before courts still unfinished. But normally, the normal standard duration would be a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. In this connection, I should like you to see a document, Mr. Kardum. That is D179.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can ask the Registry for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You will see a document which was issued by the civilian police of the United Nations on the 19th of September, 1995, which was sent to the chief, Ivan Cetina, in which document, or rather, which document says that they are submitting a list, a detailed list of all murders that were reported by UNCIVPOL from the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think this document should be under seal. I'm just reminded by my case manager. Is it the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I didn't realise it the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if need be, Mr. Registrar, a redaction should be made, and we should -- I don't know what your questions will be, Mr. -- whether we have to turn in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a gentleman from UNCIVPOL, Jan Elleby, in fact, is attaching a list in his opinion of all murders and, at the same time, requesting what the results of the investigations were, the names of suspects, any arrests made and so on and so forth. Tell me, Witness, do you know whether such requests by the civilian police of the UN were heeded by the police administration, whether they reacted to them by some communication, or did they have any contact with the police of the UN?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not reply to these letters, but we did take action pursuant to them. Now, of course, whether the chief of sector did that, whether he replied or not, I really wouldn't know, whether the Chief Cetina did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I wanted to know. Now, if we take a look at the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- and I would like to remind again that the title of this document was "Murders Reported To CIVPOL." Now, if we take a look at Item 4, it says there that on the 14th of August, a decomposed corpse was found and that the cause of death was impossible to ascertain. According to you, is this type of report or complaint sufficient to indicate that murder is in question?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. As it says there, it's impossible to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In cases as mentioned here, also in items 5, 7, 9, and so on - let's not go through all of them - but mention is made that bodies were found badly or not badly decomposed. In your experience, what is the likelihood to determine the cause of death in this state when the body is in this state, and I mean prima vista; in other words, your forensic technician, can he determine it on the site if the body involved is decomposed?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our forensic technicians did not mention the cause of death in most cases. They would usually determine that the body was decomposed, and that's what they would note. And these bodies, that is a -- most frequently, this was the case that the civilian protection actually removed such bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in such instances as mentioned here, there would be no police investigation and no processing of a case.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unless we received some subsequent information that a body found in this condition had actually been killed violently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now, I would like to refer you -- or let's now touch upon another matter, the matter of the killings or the murders in Varivode as you mentioned in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show us Document 65 ter 2638.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, the document that will come up on the screen in a minute was produced on the 3rd of October, 1995, at the 72nd battalion of the military police, and it was forwarded to the police administration of the military police, and it mentions murders in the village of Gosici. And if you take a look at this, you will see that in Gosici on the 27th of August, a multiple murder was committed and that measures were taken to investigate and to research this, and it was concluded that unidentified perpetrators who used a motor vehicle, most probably of TAM, a TAM, 2001 brand, vehicle. Now, you told us that on occasion of this murder, a police investigation was conducted as well. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall whether you had in the course of this investigation any contacts with the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move for this document to be admitted into evidence and be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D800 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could I now please have 65 ter 3158 on the screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document we're going to see now, Mr. Kardum, deals with the issue of -- of a murder in Varivode, which occurred on the 29th of September, 1995. This document also is from the military police, and the chief of this administration, Mr. Lausic, informs in it the minister of Defence of the steps taken in order to solve this crime, to solve this murder. I would now like you to look at the third paragraph, where it states that an assistant of the Ministry of the Interior informed the military structures that nine bodies of civilians were found, civilians that had been shot on the 29th of September in Varivode. And further on, it is stated that the motor vehicle that was mentioned also in the crime in the village of Gosici, the vehicle TAM 2001, camouflage -- of camouflage colour. Further on, it is noted that operational and tactical measures have been agreed as part of the criminal processing and that they will be conducted jointly by the police and the military police. Can you recall that such measures were taken and conducted together with members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even remember that the military police service was headed by Mr. Ante Glavan [phoen]. I think he was a highly placed individual in the crime service of the military police in Zadar at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to note that this document was produced on the 4th of October and that measures were taken as of the 2nd of October, once the report that a murder had been committed arrived. If we look at the second page of this document --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I would just like to say that measures were taken -- in this particular case, measures were taken on the same day, the 27th of September, so it is not true that the investigation began on the 2nd of October. Rather, it started on the 27th of September. It is possible that the crime police -- the crime military police, actually, joined in the investigation on the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I would like to discuss here. This matter here is discussed from the aspect of the military police and not the civilian police. Now, if we take a look at the fourth paragraph on the second page, it is stated there that in order to solve this multiple murder in Varivode, an operational plan of implementation was put together and that intensive searches were under way. Now, according to your rules of service, the creation of an operational and implementation plan is not done for every crime but only for crimes that are of greater significance or multiple crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this document be enter into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D801 is admitted into evidence. I have one additional question. You said that already on the 27th of September the investigations started. At the same time, I found in the document somewhere that the persons were killed on the 29th, which seems inconsistent with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. As far as I remember -- I apologise. Maybe my memory is faulty, but if I recall this, this incident was on the 27th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may be of any assistance in that matter, Your Honour, 27th of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- is the date of the incident in village Gosici, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, perhaps I have then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the problems if you have to look at these documents so quickly that...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show us Document 65 ter 3287?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, we are still examining the multiple murders in Varivode. We can see in front of us a document also produced by the military police. This document is actually a report to Major-General Mate Lausic, who is the chief of the administration, a report on what measures had been taken that far. In view of the fact that this operation of investigating the murder of -- committed in Varivode was a joint operation between the civilian and military police, I would like to ask a few questions about this. Now, first of all, we can see here the individuals who took part in this operative action, and so we can see that Mr. Franjo Djurica from the Ministry of Interior, or rather, the police was there. He was a member of the team, and he was the sector chief in the police. And then we have the crime investigation department chief, Mr. Turkalj, and Mr. Ivica Cetina, the chief of the police administration, Zadar-Knin. Have you ever participated in this operation and implementation plan in the Varivode crime?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. There's an error here. It's not Ivan Turkalj. It should be Milan Turkalj. And to answer your question, yes, with the then-assistant minister of the interior, Mr. Marijan Benko and Ivan Nadj and Milan Turkalj. I also had -- we also had the participation of two men from Zagreb, two men from Split, and we -- I also took part in the processing of this crime and also some other crimes. As far as I can recall, this team that is mentioned here was really a team that was supposed to draw up a plan of measures that should assist us in further investigations of similar crimes. So this was in support of the work of the basic -- or rather, the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But in any case, this murder, this crime received a lot of attention, and serious steps were taken to solve it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I have to repeat that the investigation was conducted by the assistant minister of the interior who was in Zadar. He was conducting it from Zadar directly where he stayed for some 25 days, up until the day when a terrorist group, Gama al Islamia, conducted an attack, a terrorist attack on the Rijeka police administration by planting a bomb, a truck -- a bomb truck there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not discuss that now. Now, if we look at page 3 of this document, we can see the measures that were taken as of 6.00 on the 7th of October up until the 10th of October. You can see that under Item 3. Identification papers of 1282 HV members were checked, and 1050 HV vehicles were searched; 17 men were searched, also HV members; and also, because of looting of property, the following HV members were brought in, and then a list of a total of 36 individuals who were brought in under suspicion of theft of property. Now, on the next page, page 4, it is also stated that the identity of 69 civilians was established; that 28 persons were removed while attempting to steal property; 11 were warned; while 9 were turned over to the Ministry of the Interior as persons caught perpetrating criminal offences of -- the criminal offence of stealing property. In Item 4, it says that in the course of this operative action, 92 staff were engaged on various tasks every day, or daily, and that the number was strengthened by 20 additional members of the anti-terrorist military police platoon. So this indicates that this was a significant operation that, of course, produced results in terms of the number of perpetrators that were discovered?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can you see from the text itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Page 5 of this document, please, Item 1, in which the murder in the village - it says here "Gorsic," but obviously this is the village of Gosici - so a murder that was committed on the 27th of August and where the description of this motor vehicle is given.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Further on, some other cases are mentioned or incidents which were investigated. This is an overall report. And in closing, in Item 6, I would like to draw your attention to the conclusion where it says that it was noted that there are facts indicating that uniforms of Croatian soldiers are abused by civilians who were actually civilians but wearing military uniforms; and also, mention is made that there have been some crimes that haven't been solved and that they were committed by members of the Croatian army. My final question regarding this document, Mr. Kardum, is the following: Is your recollection of these events consistent with what we've seen in this document here, in brief?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was produced by the military, but it is very consistent with what I remember, and I just have to say there was a similar document produced by the civilian police; in other words, in the course of our daily activities and precisely during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the reason I wanted to show you this document was precisely because this was a joint operation conducted by both the civilian and criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could I move for this document to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D802 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In view of the cooperation between the -- of the civilian police with members of the military police, do you remember that this cooperation was also manifested at joint control and check-points that were organised and set up in the territory of the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have already told us in your testimony so far something about the fact that the civilian police, in fact, did not have the authority, did not have too extensive powers vis-a-vis members of the Croatian army but in that respect required the assistance of the military police, and that was one of the reasons why the check-points that had been set up were, in fact, mixed.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If at a check-point by searching persons or some stopped vehicles it was discovered that a certain substances or things, rather, were being transported that were probably deprived from the commission of a crime, such effects would be seized, would they not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Against receipt, which was issued by the police on seized objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please look at Document 3D01-0143. You said a receipt. Now, you will see, Mr. Kardum, a specimen of a receipt on the temporary seizure of objections. We shall zoom in on it for you to see it better, and I'm going to ask you not about the content but whether this is the model of a -- the document on the basis of which items would be confiscated from persons holding such suspicion items.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A copy of this document, of this receipt would also be given to the person from whom the items were confiscated, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the other copy would be kept by the official who actually confiscated the property?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We see specifically that this is a receipt which was issued by the 7th police station in Obrovac and that a certain person -- or rather, that 40 sheep were confiscated from a certain person. This was something which was routinely done at check-points, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please move for a number for this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D803, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D803 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at another receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to mention that we collect around 500 document like this four that I intend to show just for the purposes. I don't think that it's necessary all 4 or 500, these documents, to be entered into the court file as an evidence. Maybe, it is my suggestions, that Defence could make a kind of list of these documents, and with the exchange of opinions from the Prosecution office, we could -- we could tender this -- this list as -- as a document to be in evidence from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That would be acceptable to us. Of course, a number of these confiscated items will also be reflected in crime registers and reflected in court files and other material that we've probably already submitted, so reconciliation with those other files would also be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we would have kind of a stipulation that the parties agree that 500 of these type of documents and then give some of the detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to show the type of procedure that has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps one or two examples, then, attached to it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will give four examples just for the purposes of what I have just been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now we have, of course, the problems with the translations from that amount of documents, it is obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the advantages of forms, that they usually have the same language, all them. But of course, what is filled in by hand is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates your effort to keep the number of pages within limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can I ask the Registry to show us Document 3D01-0145, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We shall see a similar, or rather, an identical form, a receipt issued in this case by the police station in Gracac where also an automatic rifle, nine calves which were being transported on such-and-such truck with such-and-such licence plates were confiscated from a person. What I should like to draw your attention to, Mr. Kardum, is the fact that this person was stopped at the Stikade military check-point. Can we then conclude that in this case this is -- in this case we had members of the regular police together with the military police manning this check-point?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have a number for this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D804 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at Document 3D01-0149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document we are about to see is practically identical, an identical form, however, this time issued by the 72nd Battalion of the military police. And it states that such-and-such soldier -- that items were confiscated from such-and-such soldier with number -- serial number 9 inclusive. Mr. Kardum, the way you perceive this, this is an identical example to the previous two which we have just seen except that it was issued by the military criminal police, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because -- because Zlatko Lopac is a soldier, and it is so written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please move that this document be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D805 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another one which is very similar to those first document that I entered, so I don't think that it's necessary to...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Kardum, we saw in which way the check-points functioned, the check-point blockades. If it would be established by further processing that the -- there -- the confiscated items had been stolen, then you would also file a criminal complaint?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In fact, I saw that there was the mark "KU 83" on one of these receipts meaning that already at that moment, that particular case already had been the subject of a criminal complaint filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the receipt that we have just entered as evidence, D803. Obviously, that receipt was part of a criminal file and as material evidence was actually treated as such in the procedure before the competent court, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before the document disappears from our screen, D -- I think it's D805, it says receipt for temporarily confiscated items, and then we find them listed. What made the confiscation of a temporary nature? Could the witness perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I could cover that topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would cover that. That's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard His Honour's question. This receipt says that the items confiscated are temporarily confiscated.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. All the receipts issued by the police were issued on standard uniform forms. Now, the final decision whether the item in question would be seized for good or not would be brought by court. We would just indicate that there was the ground of suspicion that it might have been the subject of a criminal offence, but the final decision was on the police. But we can see here on the left side that this particular receipt already has a number, a criminal complaint number, which is KU 156, meaning that a complaint had already been filed by the crime police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps have the original moved up a bit so that we have -- that we can view -- yes, now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think we have a problem with the translation, Your Honour. Just -- my learned colleague reminded me of that, as it regards to the -- who is -- who was authorised to reach the final decision referring to the confiscated items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could perhaps ask the witness to tell us. Who finally was the authority -- who was authorised to make the final decision in relation to the confiscated items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court, exclusively the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. We could proceed, Your Honour, if you don't have any further question on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have, as a matter of fact, a question which is triggered by the last answer of the witness. Now, receipt means that this document was given to the person from whom items were temporarily confiscated. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those items were confiscated by the police, and it would take them into custody. As a rule, they were to be delivered with -- against a criminal complaint to the district attorney, but in practice there was no rule where these officers would store all that so that the police kept them in custody and very often in these situations gave them to government commissioners, which is to say to the people in charge in the municipalities. But in some cases, they could also give it to some persons in the case of theft of wood, for instance, or something which is of bulky nature that would be kept by the person in question, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not perfectly clear now. I understand a receipt to be that someone signs or makes a record of objects being handed over to another person. Now, who is here transferring the objects to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police hands over these objects to the district attorney with a criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The confiscated items, as a rule, with the filed criminal complaint given by the police to the district attorney. But as here we have bulky, voluminous things such as tiles or wooden barrels that is not possible because of practical considerations. That's why the police either keeps them in their own -- on its own premises or has them stored elsewhere, but in situations like these sometimes they would be entrusted to the perpetrator, or rather, to the suspect to keep them until further notice. And that person was under the obligation to keep such things until the final resolution of his case, when voluminous objects were in question, large, bulky objects. If these were -- that -- it was jewellery or some smaller items, they would also be transferred to the district attorney's office with the criminal complaint or would have been kept in the premises of the police station in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the last line reads in English: "The aforementioned items placed in safekeeping with the subject." I do not fully understand what that means. Could we have a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, these items were given to that person for safekeeping or to keep them, to have them in his custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, soldier Zlatko Lopac, finally, was in charge of keeping those goods, or is that how I have to understand it, because they were confiscated temporarily from him? And now the aforementioned items placed in safekeeping with the subject, is that the person where these items were confiscated from? Is that how I have to understand the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic. I'm just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's maybe -- it's maybe ambiguous on the first sight, but we will cover this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kardum, this receipt in fact shows that a certain number of items were found on a certain person and they have been listed, enumerated. You said due to practical considerations, the voluminosity of these items, they simply could not be sent to the district attorney as such; and therefore, that person was ordered to keep them and could not alienate them, could not sell them or in any other way dispose of them until the procedure was over?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So these are purely practical reasons and not legal considerations?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is the practice today as well. This is the routine practice today, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The items that were less voluminous would be rather -- would be submitted to the district attorney's office in charge against a complaint or would have been kept in storage under supervision?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the district attorney always knew where the objects were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me now try to fully understand this document. This is a list of rather large objects, wooden barrel, 150-litre capacity, something that you just do not carry away; same true for three wall kitchen cabinets. Now, let's take this example. Where would these objects have found? Where was it established that Mr. -- Soldier Zlatko Lopac was in possession of these items? How would that have been established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, we will have to consult the entire list; that is, KU 95-19697. Obviously Soldier Zlatko Lopac was transporting these items on a lorry, I presume, or in a van. Obviously, he had stolen them in the occupied territory, taken them simply from somewhere in the occupied territory and was unable to prove their origin, where he got them in a legal, lawful manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So he was stopped somewhere, and you need, really, a little truck to transport all these items. Yes. Now, what would then happen to these items? Would they be taken by the police, or was the person just allowed to keep them for that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on how far this was from any place where it could be stored in a warehouse. So for practical considerations, however, from the legal standpoint, everything was done as should be. The soldier signed that the items were confiscated. Also, the authorised person signed a document, and it was sealed. And of course, the district attorney was informed of it. So the -- the only issue that remained unresolved was where these item would say be kept until it was finally resolved legally what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at that very moment -- I'm just trying to imagine what happens. I see a little truck being stopped with all these goods in it. Now -- so at that moment the person who's transporting these the goods is unable to establish that he is the rightful owner of these items. Was it at that moment that such a document would be made or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It would be made there on the spot, and the person would be taken in for processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what happened, then, with the goods? Because he was still in charge of the goods, isn't it? Would he take them ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily, Your Honour. He would be taken in for processing. In other words, the police - in this case, the military police, but otherwise, it could be the civilian police as well - they would try to determine where he got this from. They would interview him where he got the items from, which village, what house, and so on and so forth. However, here, obviously, this was property of some owners who had abandoned their homes. I assume that most probably these were Serbs that had fled the area, and I doubt that it was possible at all to determine the owner, the rightful owner of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say such a document was created on the spot where this person was stopped and where it was established that he was transporting so many goods. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The items would be put on -- listed on a list. The person would sign this document that it was actually confiscated from him; and in fact, this is a very powerful -- very powerful evidence. This is an exhibit for the Court, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now what would then happen? Police officers there would -- what would the next step be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person would then be taken in to the closest police station, and the crime processing would begin. This person would be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He would be interviewed immediately after he was stopped and after this document would have been made. Where would the goods, meanwhile, be? Because they were in his truck. Would the truck be taken to the police station, as well, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, before being taken in, you said this is a case where a court number -- I think you said a court number was already assigned. How would you assign a number -- I'll just check what exactly your words were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think he said court number, Your Honour. He said KU number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- therefore, I'm verifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a police number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the police number would be assigned on the street where they were -- where these goods were found in the possession of this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the police obviously determined that it was -- that a crime had been committed; in this case, aggravated crime or aggravated theft. The policeman would call his duty service and request the next free number -- next available number in the register, the police register, the KU number. So most probably, this number was assigned as KU or the crime number, crime register number, 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he would, then, be taken to the police station, and after he had been processed, after he had been interviewed, he would then leave again and be the one who should look after the goods so that they would remain in his possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. In this instance, they would -- in cases such as these, they would have to actually discuss with the direct attorney whether a red crime report should be written out, in which case he would have to be taken in. If it was a regular procedure, then there would be a white crime report, in which case this person would not be detained. And everything that I have said actually refers to civilians. Now, this is a military case, and it may be that the military procedure is a bit different to that of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would the difference be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know the details of the procedure of the military police. I think it was a similar procedure, but I'm not absolutely sure because I didn't work on this case with them from beginning to end. Because you can see here that mention is made that the 71st Company of the military police, actually -- or the military crime police was the one who investigated this. So this case was investigated by the military police, not the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for -- yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just for a clarification. I could point out at D804, which is the very same receipt, where the truck has been mentioned in which the supposedly stolen goods were found. So in the D805, there was no mention any truck, but obviously it has to be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you'll understand what the purpose of my questions is to better understand what happens. If we have 500 documents in which it says that the person who apparently was suspected of having stolen them keeps them, then of course it becomes a very interesting question what then happened afterwards. It might be misinterpreted by other persons to see that people continue to transport these objects, and then, of course, the follow-up issue of whether ever a court decision on the final confiscation took place. I mean, this is a whole complex --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- matter for which, of course, to fully understand what those 500 documents you will list together with Mr. Margetts what it actually tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I can assure that the Defence will cover there topic in a total -- of course, in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So from the very beginning where the stolen -- supposedly stolen goods were temporarily confiscated up to the final court decision on the matter. So in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Kind of a chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would just draw the Court's attention again to D511 and D568 where you do have final results of -- not necessarily concretely these particular confirmations, but do you have what happened to the cases afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we have not fully analysed all this material yet, but since -- as the witness here could tell us about the procedures that I take the opportunity, also, to hear from the witness and not only study documents. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kardum, we will now broach the last topic that I have for you, and that is the special police. Within the Zadar-Knin police administration, there was a unit of the special police as we saw in Exhibit P500, the commander of which was Mr. Vrsajko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your 2004 statement, you said -- and may I refer you to paragraph - just a minute, please - paragraph 52. You said that you did not have too many contacts with the special police because these were combat units. Is that a good interpretation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to meet with Mr. Vrsajko frequently. However, the nature of his work and that of mine were very different, so we didn't really overlap a lot except in the cases where we cooperated and we had a fair, decent cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your 2004 statement, you said that as far as you understood the check-points were later -- some check-points were later manned by special and military police. Did you actually ever see members of a combat unit such as the special police at check-points?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is a misinterpretation or mistranslation, but did you actually mean military police or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this referred to the military police. The military police would in those cases handle military persons, and the civilian police would handle civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But there were no members of the special police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can recall, no, because all the competences that were within the authority, the powers of the special police were also within the competence of the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you told us at the outset -- when you began your testimony, you said that you didn't have any contacts with Mr. Markac. You also just told us just now that you didn't have any contacts with the special police because your work was different. Now, I would like to ask you this in closing: Have you ever in your experience received an order from anyone in the chain of command not to investigate, an order banning or forbidding an investigation that you were authorised to undertake by law?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, if someone were to issue such an order to you, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were issued such an order - and I'm just trying to think of that -- such a situation, hypothetic situation - I would first inform my immediate superior and ask him to tell me what his position was. And if he agreed to that order, then I would request to have it in writing; and most probably, I would resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in interpreting what you have said that your position was that you would always act within the bounds of law and no one could issue any orders to the contrary of that?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kardum, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I please call up 1D54-0001, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, while we're waiting for that to come up on the screen, I have put together maps of your area of responsibility, which we're going to show on the screen, and I'm going to ask you to look at the maps and see if we have put this down on paper accurately. You'll note on the first page, sir, the -- and I will note the Court, there is, I believe, an English translation, but we will use the Croatian version for the benefit of the witness. The brown line marks the international border with Bosnia and Herzegovina; the green line are the Kotar-Knin boundary line; and the yellow line is the boundary of the police administration of Zadar-Knin. Does that accurately depict the -- your area of responsibility in the police administration, Zadar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now what we've done, Mr. Kardum, is include the police stations. You'll see the -- a red circled -- red circles with the yellow are the police stations within Kotar-Knin; the blue circles are the police stations that are not part of the Kotar-Knin administration; and the black circle is the location of the police administration itself. And I'd ask you to take a look at this map carefully and see if we've accurately depicted the various police stations and the police administration on this map.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But I would have a few corrections to make, if necessary, if you feel it appropriate. I think I should comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I won't be -- all right. The police station Kistanje, for instance, it existed as such and was operational. However, I think that it was not within the police system, but in the day-to-day work there was a need to have regular police between Benkovac and Knin, that area. So then we decided to have an ad hoc outpost, police outpost in Kistanje, which was an outpost of the Knin first police station. In other words, a police branch or police outpost is of lower rank than the police station, but I think that in the original document it was not envisaged as -- as existing. As for the rest, it is all right except that these blue ones at the Kotar-Knin PU are border police, and the border police stations are different in their work. They're different in their work to the ones that you marked with the red circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And just to clarify, we did put the dates in of when these police stations were opened up, and they're located on the map as well. So what I'm asking you is, these police stations actually did exist in the month of August as part of your police administration, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, what we've done in the third slide is added -- first of all, that black line, we've already in this case shown what the border was between the Split Military District and the Gospic Military District. You might not be familiar with that, but that's drawn in on this slide. The blue line is the line held by the HV on the 3rd of August, 1995; and the red line is the line held by the ARSK on the 3rd of August, 1995. Do you agree that that is your understanding of where the front lines were on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never looked at a similar map to this one, but to the best of my recollection, I think, yes, that that fully corresponds to the actual state of affairs then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking at this map and looking at the yellow line, is it fair to say that the majority of the occupied territory in Sector South fell under the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this morning I wanted to put some numbers together for you, and I'm sure the Court will correct me and will check my math later. But prior to Operation Storm, is it your understanding or do you have an understanding that the actual area that your police administration covered - in other words, the actual area held by Croatian authorities on the 3rd of August - covered roughly 1200 square kilometres? Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the area of the former municipalities of Zadar and Biograd. Biograd has about 260 and Zadar somewhat under a thousand square kilometres, these two former municipalities, and that is exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, do you recall that your area of responsibility - and by "your," I mean the police administration Zadar-Knin - expanded roughly five times what it had before Operation Storm to cover roughly 6350 square kilometres of territory? Is that a fair representation of how much your zone of responsibility expanded after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We were a second-rank administration, and the Zagreb police administration and the Split and Dalmatia administrations were of the first rank. Then we became territorially larger, both from the Zagreb administration and the Split-Dalmatia administration taken together. I often asked my chief, Cetina, then to see to it from our Ministry of the Interior that we should become an administration of the first rank, which would mean a much large number of people and much more resources, et cetera. But this request could not be accommodated so that this administration was reorganised, and a part of the people went to Gospic where they had belonged before, and another part went to Sibenik, to which they had also belonged before. I apologise for this comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, based on some of the answers you gave both to Mr. Margetts and Mr. Mikulicic, we've established that you had as a high number 60 people working as your subordinates in the crime investigation section. I've done the math, and, again, I trust that there are people in this courtroom who will correct me if I'm wrong, but if you assigned all 60 -- or sorry. If you had these people, and you took -- you did two shifts and had 30 people per shift out in the field, and none of them were interviewing POWs at the POW centre. Before Operation Storm, one shift, one person could cover 40 square kilometres of territory, which is 1200 square kilometres divided by 30; and after Operation Storm, one of your subordinates had to cover 212 square kilometres of territory. Now, is it fair to say, Mr. Kardum, that your police administration was not adequately equipped to deal with the situation it found itself in when its territorial jurisdiction expanded five times its size in a matter of days?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I thank you for such a precise math. I do have to add that at the very beginning of the Oluja operation I lost four people, four of my men, three of them on account of an incident which they had made, and there was a senior lady, operations officer who had a traffic accident that morning, so that that number was further reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, you are familiar with Operative Action Povratak, are you not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Operative Action Povratak began in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Croatian plans under OA Povratak were based on the principle that the Vance Plan would be implemented and that Serbian police officers would in fact remain in place when Croatian authority was restored over the occupied area?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that the MUP did not anticipate a situation where all the police staff in the occupied area would leave?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when we talk about the difficulties that you encountered - and I believe you mentioned this in your testimony earlier - in establishing the police administration in the crime investigative section, the first and fundamental point was you didn't have enough people to do everything that was required of you in terms of investigations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, before the break - let me just go over this issue - we went through the issue of the receipt a few minutes ago, and you were saying something about the practicality problem. My question to you, sir, is: Was it your experience that if police officers, either civil or military, were out in some remote area of the police administration, wasn't it the case that sometimes given the lack of resources at that time that all the police could do at the check-point was issue a receipt and follow up with the perpetrator later because you didn't have enough men to take off the check-point to escort everybody to the police station for every criminal act. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite true. But that receipt was always issued in two copies, and a copy was kept and another was given to the person in question so that we could always follow at all times whether the person in question acted on instructions given him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my question -- specific question is: Was it not the case that if a police officer at a check-point took every person in that was stopped at the check-point with having committed some criminal act, that the check-points themselves wouldn't be manned because of the shortage of police officers to cover the check-points? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, I do. But the -- the check-points were priority points that were not to be abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President. I think this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is, but not before I have put an additional question. I asked you earlier, Mr. Kardum, what would happen if a person was stopped and where it was established that he was transporting these goods? You told me that -- you told this Chamber that the items would be put on a list, person would sign the document, and you said, This is very powerful evidence. And then I said: What would next happen? Police officers there would -- what would the next step be? You said this person would then be taken into the closest police station and the crime processing would begin. That is an answer which is quite different from the last answers you gave to Mr. Misetic. I asked you without even suggesting what the next step would be, and you said they would be taken in. Now, Mr. Misetic and -- ask you, Well, wouldn't that be bad for the check-point? Wouldn't it be true that -- and then you said, no, the check-point should not be abandoned. Now, please tell me, were these people taken in as you told me? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Misetic said if this check-point was quite far, quite remote from the police station. So if this was a check-point which was quite far from the police station because these are large areas that we're talking about here. For instance, between the police station in Knin and the close police station in the direction of Zadar, Benkovac, you have about 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what a long distance is. Now -- so therefore, your answer to my question should have been: It depends. Sometimes they would be taken in; sometimes they would not. Could you tell me, how -- what would be approximately the percentage of those who would have been stopped with items on their trucks which they could not explain as being their own -- being their property? What would be the percentage that would be taken in, and what would be the percentage of those who were so far that it was just making a list and then not taking them? Would 5 per cent be taken in? Would 60 per cent be taken in? Would 80 per cent be taken in? Would 30 per cent be taken in? Approximately. Of course, I do not ask you to give a precise percentage, but approximately. Let's start with the first question. Would the majority be taken in, or would the majority not be taken in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The majority would be taken in but not by the people manning the check-points. Other police, most often crime police members would come to get them if civilians were in question because the criminal police was stationed in the police stations. I said before that there were four or five of them in Benkovac who covered Benkovac, Obrovac, and Stankovci; four or five of them in Knin in that period who covered the area of Knin; and four of five of them in Gracac who covered the area of Gracac, Lapac, and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say the majority was taken in, mainly not by those manning the check-points but by other police officers. Were there sufficient police officers available to go to the check-point, take them in and -- or was there any problem as far as the number of available police officers was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that depended on the daily events because the daily incidents, daily events also impacted the possibilities of such officers to come and get these persons. But as a rule, most frequently they would be taken in. But it is also depended on the tape and nature, the severity, the gravity of the criminal offence because there were people who were just smuggling or transporting, rather, one sheep or one lamb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would, then, such a list, although a very short list, be made, as well, for one sheep or one lamb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We filed criminal complaints even in such cases. Of course, these persons would often say this comes from my relative or this is from my friend, it was given to me by a friend of mine, and similar excuses and this dragged on for -- - ad infinitum, but we always proceeded in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told us that the majority would be taken in. Could you be more precise? Would -- 80 per cent, would it be a vast majority that would be taken in or just a little bit over half? Could you give us further position as far as the percentage of persons taken in is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is difficult for me to say. There are documents, case files, and each case file shows whether the person in question was taken in on the same day and interviewed on the same day. But a free estimation that I could make is that perhaps 70 per cent or more of such persons were taken in in this or that way, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I forgot to tender the slides as an exhibit, and I ask that they be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit number D806, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D806 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I may now have Exhibit D9 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you look on the screen, this is an exhibit that was admitted with a witness earlier in this case. It is a criminal report regarding the murder of Sava Babic, and I'd ask to you take a look at that page, and then we'll turn to the next page when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 6 in the English, which is also page 6 in the Croatian, I believe. When you finish reading it, we'll turn to the next page, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, do you recall investigating the murder of Sava Babic?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall preparing a criminal report in that case, which I've shown you, as well as a special report in that case?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall sending the special report, in which it was suspected that a soldier by the name of Mario Dukic, a member of the 134th Home Guard brigade -- do you recall sending that special report to the military - sorry - to the military prosecutor in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm using this example. I'd like to you explain, given that you recall the investigation how it is that the investigation was begun and why it is that you filed a special report with the military prosecutor in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. We had an incident, a murder that occurred I think also in September in a village near Benkovac. I can't remember with certainty the name of that place, but I'll probably remember it as I speak. A civilian of Serb nationality was killed then. His name was Petar Botar. When we conducted an investigation, we found out that three men committed the murder. These men were of Croat ethnicity. One of them was Mario Dukic, and I think that at this time he was a member of the 134th Home Guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Regiment, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when we learned of that fact, then the military police also participated in the investigation, and Mario Dukic and other two men were brought in. I can't claim with certainty, but I think the other two were civilians. During the investigation, it turned out that the murder had been committed under the influence of alcohol by Mario Dukic. I just need to add something, although it has nothing to do with this murder. Petar Botar is the father of Branko Botar, a perpetrator of a war crime at the detriment of a Croat woman during the occupation of that territory, a woman from Perusic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or that person is from Perusic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this occasion, we proved that Mario Dukic committed this murder with a 7.62-millimetre pistol, and now I can say for certain which murder occurred first. But because we found a shell, a 7.62-millimetre shell on the crime scene where Babic was murdered, we sent this shell to Zagreb for a forensic examination, and after a while, this -- we received a report from Zagreb that Petar Botar and Sava Babic were murdered by -- from the same weapon or with the same weapon, fire-arm, and it was concluded that the perpetrator was Mario Dukic.
