As a result, we prepared a special report and filed it with the military prosecutor because Mario was, at this time -- at the time when this crime was committed, he was a member of, as far as I can recall, 134th regiment, Home Guard regiment. Mr. Attorney, if you do have any more questions I can answer them. I just don't want to take up too much of your time with my length explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in now is you've explained that at some point because you had established that Mario Dukic had committed a separate murder with a 7.62-millimetre shell and because you found the same type shell at the murder scene of Sava Babic, you suspected that Mario Dukic was involved in the murder of Sava Babic at that point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, MUP, in your office, even though you suspected that Mario Dukic, a member of the 134th Home Guard Brigade, had committed the murder, MUP was still responsible for continuing the investigation of the murder of Sava Babic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this point in time, we didn't know that he was the perpetrator of the murder of Sava Babic. It was only later that we confirmed this because all the weapons and the cartridges that were found -- the cartridge that was found on the site of the murder of Sava Babic, it was found that this cartridge was fired from the same pistol from which the other person was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Understood, but --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Botar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- what I would like to know is, MUP carries out its investigations of a crime until it confirms a suspect, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it's only after MUP has established probable cause that a suspect of a crime such as murder is a member of the Croatian army that the military police is then called in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. So what we are looking at is the crime itself, and then only secondarily, the perpetrator, because we don't know who the perpetrator might be. For us, there is a crime, and that has to be resolved, and the perpetrator may be a civilian, a military person. We don't know that at that point in time. If it's a member of the Croatian army, then there's a specific approach. We have a duty to inform thereof the competent military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've answered that you were looking at the crime itself and then only secondarily, the perpetrator, and that's the point I want to talk about. Crime that's committed in the liberated territory, it is MUP's task under Croatian law to investigate every crime and to gather evidence that would lead to the conclusion as to who the suspect is in that crime, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, if at the very outset the perpetrator is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us -- give us an example where at the very beginning you know who the perpetrator is.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, at check-points, if one were to see a military person transporting some stolen goods, then we would -- we would register this as OP, the immediately known perpetrator; NN is unidentified perpetrator; and the NO is subsequently discovered perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let's take the situation now: A body is discovered, and the -- an immediately known perpetrator -- in other words, the perpetrator is not still physically on the scene when the body is discovered. It is MUP's job to carry out the investigation if there's a basis do believe that there was violence involved in the death of that person, to carry out the investigation that would lead to establishing who is suspected of that crime, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, even after you've identified a suspect such as Mario Dukic after an investigation and you've called in the military police, MUP still has a role in the investigation, does it not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then we worked on it together. You could say that we cooperated. I think the military did not have specialised men for such criminal acts and that it wasn't capable of conducting this investigation on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So it was the MUP that had the specialisation pathologists, ballistic experts, other type of expertise to provide in assisting the military police in eventually prosecuting a crime before a military Court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. It was not a MUP that had the pathologist and the experts, et cetera. The experts were independent experts. The pathologists were physicians of a special -- having a specialisation who could be recruited only at the order of the investigating judge, not at the order of the police. So following an order of the investigating judge, we could recruit the services of a physician, a pathologist, and they he would then be assigned his particular assignment by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take the example of Mario Dukic and the murder of Sava Babic. Who conducts the -- who conducted in that particular case the ballistics analysis and any other type of expertise that was done in that case?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expertise was undertaken by the competent experts in the centre, the only such centre which existed at the time in Croatia which was called Ivan Vucetic and was in Zagreb. It was an independent centre, I think. At least that's it how it should have been and should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was a civilian investigative judge involved in the investigation of the murder of Sava Babic?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the investigation of the murder of Petar Botar participated an investigating judge and a district attorney, but that murder was practically solved by the expert. The expert solved it on the basis of what the investigating judge and the police had recovered at the scene of the murder. During the on-site investigation, we found inter alia a cartridge, and we sent that cartridge not knowing the perpetrator for ballistic analysis in Zagreb. After a couple of months, we, the police, received the expert report of the expert from which it stemmed that on the occasion of the murder of Sava Babic the same weapon was used as the one that was used in the case of Petar Botar, and we had already detected the -- or solved the murder of Petar Botar earlier, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question. Is it your understanding that the jurisdiction for investigating crime where the specific perpetrator's identity is unknown rests with MUP and that the jurisdiction of the military police under Croatian law at that time only existed once the identity of the perpetrator was confirmed as someone who is a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'm going to show two exhibits now to the witness and then ask a few questions. If I could have 1D54-0012, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a criminal report filed by you for the Gosici murders. Can you just take a look at it and see if this is the document that you prepared on 4 October.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the next page, please. Yes. This is a document which was produced in the criminal police department of the Zadar-Knin police administration. It is my signature. Actually, it is typewritten that it is my signature, but this was a signed propria persona and by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D807 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D54-0007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, this is the criminal report you filed in the Varivode case. I'd ask you to look through this document and see if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this document just as in the first case, I mean, in the case of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D808.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D808 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'd now like to call up 1D54-0017, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you could take a look at this and read through it and tell me when you're finished. This is a criminal report you filed against a Nino Starcevic, whom you identified as a soldier. I believe it has to do with a theft. If you could take a look at it, and the date is 1 September --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The date is 1 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there's also a second perpetrator identified in your report as a member of the 4th Guards Brigade and that these two gentlemen committed the criminal offence of taking a motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page, please. Now, it says "Ive Kardum" on the bottom. Is that someone who was authorised to sign for you there?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was signed by Ante Pogarilic. In these police stations - I have to explain this - Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, Lapac, Korenica, I was supposed to have a number of staff, 19 in each of these stations, and at the head of them should have been the deputy chief of crime police. And this person was should have had the authority to sign criminal complaints. However, since the whole service had not been set up properly, there weren't -- there simply did not exist -- these people did not exist, the deputy crime police chief, so that it was -- so that these jobs were done by other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could explain here for the Court, the perpetrator of the first one is identified as a soldier; the second one is identified as member of the 4th Guards Brigade. Can you explain to us how it is that you -- or someone authorised on your behalf filed this criminal report for theft against persons who are identified as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was probably done in agreement with the military police because I saw here at the very bottom of page 2 where it says that the official interview was done with the -- in the presence of the military police with Ante Zilic, so I assume that the civilian police asked the military police to conduct the interview with Ante Zilic and vice versa, and they probably agreed that the complaint would be filed by the civilian police. I'm not even sure that this is the proper procedure, the way they did it, but the point was the job had to be done, and it was. Now, whether a mistake had been made, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it says who it was delivered to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page -- or to the bottom -- next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says to the Zadar municipal state attorney's office, the analytics department, the department of organised crime prevention, and to the archive. So the criminal report wasn't filed with the military prosecutor or the military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in my view, that's a mistake. It's a procedural error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It would be your understanding as according to your earlier testimony that the MUP could investigate this incident; once they'd identified these three individuals as perpetrators who were members of the HV, you would call in the military police to actually do the arrest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could -- I will tender this exhibit into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D809 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, I'd like to take a hypothetical example. An HV soldier, active duty, gets intoxicated, sits behind the wheel of a car in Zadar, and gets involved in a fatal car accident, which results in the death of another motorist, civilian. When MUP arrives at the scene, what is MUP's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the arrest of that member of the -- that army member would be arrested. Then the MUP would also have to inform the military police of that arrest of the incident, that they had arrested a member of the army, that such a report would be also sent to the district attorney, to the investigative judge. The investigating judge would conduct an on-site investigation unless it is entrusted to the civilian police. If entrusted to the civilian police, it will conduct the on-site investigation; and then in agreement with the military police, further investigating measures would be taken, and the district attorney would ask the competent court to conduct an investigation. Talking about this, some things which were carried out by the police, even if by mistake, even if the police mischaracterized a criminal offence, if it characterized a criminal offence as aggravated theft whereas it was robbery or sent it to a not-competent tier of the system, that is considered an error. But this is not a particular error in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who -- first, you said that the army member would be arrested. Who conducts the initial arrest in Zadar of that HV soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police that happens to be first at the scene of the event or closest to the scene of the event, if you're referring to either the military or the civilian police, the police that is first there. Such a -- we cannot let such a man irrespective of the fact that he's a member of the Croatian army, we cannot allow him to escape, to continue doing foolish things or to try and conceal his criminal offences, et cetera, because we don't want him to escape. We want to prove that he was intoxicated or the presence of alcohol in his organism, if that was the case, and then we would inform the military police, and then we would agree with them on the further course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who secures the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The scene of the crime would be secured. I don't know how relevant that is, but I think it would be the civilian police, but then again, it might be the military police because this is a military person. It can be the civilian police or the military police or a combination of both police forces. It will not be only the military police. Of that, I'm certain because the victim is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I have D97 on the screen, please. Your Honours, we are -- we will give a hard copy of D97 to the witness in Croatian. I noticed that there was a -- a translation error in the English of D97 because it was missing one section, which I would like to ask the witness about, and we, therefore, will show the amended version on Sanction, upload the right version into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I hear of no objections. Of course, I do not know whether the new translation has been uploaded already, whether you have had an opportunity to review it, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I haven't had an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But may I take it that...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've sent it to Prosecution as part of our disclosure here. I think we -- Your Honour pointed it out back when we tendered the exhibit and it wasn't -- it was never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that if a completed translation is provided by the parties, that that could -- that we could start working on that basis, and if there would be any objections, that we would hear after it has been verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think you'll see that it's -- I don't think there's going to be any dispute about it so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's at Tab number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We put it at 14 in our disclosures to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you could take a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report from Minister Jarnjak to the state prosecutor, Marijan Hranjski, dated 2 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please. And just so the Court is aware, what was missing before is under "Known Perpetrators." It was blank. The three boxes were blank. We just put them in so that it's reflected in the new translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the second page, Mr. Kardum, you will see that Minister Jarnjak informs the state prosecutor of certain statistics, and he reports that for the period of 22 August to 2 October 1995, in the police administration Zadar-Knin, he reports 28 murders, 162 burnings, 3 for mining, and 132 cases of removal of property. And if we go down to the next graph or next table, it says, Zadar-Knin, 192 on-site investigations were conducted during that roughly 6-week time-period. The known perpetrators, MUP had identified 28 HV members, 194 civilian perpetrators, and 1 abuse of uniform with 15 unknown perpetrators. Now, the first question is, can you tell us what "abuse of uniform" means?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a frequently encountered problem in that period. Namely, civilians would put on military uniforms and were not members of the army or of the police. There were less such cases in terms of the abuse of police uniforms. Most frequently these cases involved the abuse of military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it consistent with your recollection that the Zadar-Knin police administration conducted 192 on-site investigations during that time-period. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This seems a small number to me. I think that we had more onsite investigations conducted, and the number of reported people was larger but depends on when the data was received, when the information was finally computer-processed, et cetera, because at that time we were only establishing our computer database and system, so that -- perhaps that might account for that. Otherwise, we in the police have this practice that we have to finish all the paperwork within a month, so that has to be done by the 4th or 5th of the month. I notice here that the date given is the 2nd of October. I believe that I saw in the earlier criminal complaints that both Gosici and Varivode were processed on the 4th of October so that these complaints were written later. Therefore, I don't know whether the information on the then-murder was also entered in the statistics process by the police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But do you also agree that for that time-period that the MUP had identified 28 HV members as -- at least 28 HV members as known perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Kardum, I'd like to take you back to your 2004 statement, which is P896, page 6 in the English, please. And this is at paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you would read the transcript, after the "Q" for "Question," you will see often "Previous translation continues." Could I ask you to make a pause as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I don't know if Mr. Margetts has had a chance to review it, but I'm reminded to ask for permission from the Chamber to replace the English translation that's currently with D97 with the corrected version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I haven't had a chance to review it properly. I'll attempt to do so at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's just the three categories added, unless we -- may I take it that if I would look at the original, which I have not done yet, it might well be that I could immediately, myself, verify whether this comes close to what apparently is added to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I have attempted to do that in the binder but haven't found the original. I've sent an e-mail to just some other staff to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can inform counsel that the erroneous page was one we picked up from 65 ter 4444, so you should be able to find the original uploaded there, and then we made the correction now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence is allowed to upload, and if there's any problem, we'd like to hear from you within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, at paragraph 33 of your 2004 statement, the first sentence says: "After Operation Storm, we in the civilian police could only conduct investigations where the military were not suspected." That's not accurate, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely not true. I can tell you exactly what the actual sense of this should be. What paragraph did you say this was?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, we in the civilian police could conduct investigations until it was established that the perpetrator of a criminal offence was a military up to that point. Once it was established that it was a member of the military that was the perpetrator, we were to inform the military police, and the military police would then in accordance with the legal regulations seize itself of the matter and continue the investigation, and we would then further agree on the further procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We need to clarify this point further. It's -- it's not simply that you -- once you identify that the suspect was in the military but that you specifically identify the perpetrator by his identity and that he is a member of the military. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that that is fully correct. The moment we arrived at the conclusion that the perpetrator could be a military, we would have to seek the assistance of the military police in order to get to that person and interview that person. I don't know whether you understand me. Namely, I believe that I gave a fuller response to this question when I said that the criminal offence was what was meritorious for us. It was not the perpetrator but the criminal offence that we were guided by. When we had probable cause to believe that someone could be associated with a criminal offence, we had to deal with that in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: However, in a situation where the identity of a perpetrator is unknown for an unknown crime, let's say you found a body, it would not be enough for you to stop an investigation because you suspect that the murder might have been committed by someone in a military uniform, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. That is just an assumption. In respect of every killed person, one could assume that the perpetrator might have been this or that person, a civilian or a military. It could have been under, inverted commas, the friendly side, or some people could have been -- some Serbs could have been killed by Serbs. We just have the criminal offence. We do not have the perpetrator yet, and of course, the civilian police is the competent one to act. But we did make a distinction here in a certain way between all those events which were not connected to combat. But if we knew about some combat activities directly, for instance, if we came to Knin, the police came there on the 6th of August, and we find an enemy soldier dead, we would not investigate such a case. That would be handled by the sanitization or civilian protection crew, and they would be responsible -- except, of course, if we found out later that that body had been the victim of a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I was also looking at the clock. I'm aware that quite a few questions were put by the Bench. Could you give us an indication as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will try to wrap up in 30 minutes, Your Honour, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you would then, also, go over the one hour and 30 minutes you indicated, but we'll ask Mr. Registrar to give full and detailed information, including... Then we'll have a break. We'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like just to inform the Chamber that I -- for the rest of the week I wouldn't be present in the courtroom due to some emergency that occurs suddenly, and my absence, of course, with the consent of our client, Mr. Kuzmanovic will take care of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope that the emergency is not of a sad nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is, but I'll be back on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we feel sorry for the emergency being of a sad nature for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think you're two minutes off from your one hour and a half according to the registrar. Could you please finish within the next 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you've have heard I have 20 minutes, so I need you to be very succinct in your answers, and we'll get through this material. You described in the Varivode case and in the Gosici case that a type of task force was created with the MUP and the military police. Why wasn't General Gotovina asked to be a member of the task force?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said before, we never contacted officers other than the military police. We exclusively worked with the military police. Furthermore, at the time in question, I don't even know where General Gotovina was, and I never communicated with him, and if there were someone to communicate with him it would have been someone at a higher level. We contacted the military police alone. We generally contacted lower level officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time in the Varivode or Gosici case where you recall somebody saying, we need to involve the commander of the Military District in the investigation, given that we suspect that soldiers were involved?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that ever anything like that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will save time. I was going to play a video, Mr. Kardum, which was D508, and it is Minister Jarnjak at a press conference on the 8th of August when he was asked a question about allegations that the Bosnian army had crossed over into Croatia and burned some villages down. If I may summarize, Minister Jarnjak said the police will go in, secure the area, conduct an investigation, and take appropriate steps once the perpetrator is identified. Why weren't more incidents of burning in your area of responsibility investigated in August/September 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already tried to explain this earlier. We were very busy with the tasks that we had at the very outset. Even before these incidents of burning of houses, we were given priority tasks, which were to secure the reception centres; to find mass graves where people, Croats had been buried during the occupation; finding and marking the minefields in order to prevent civilians from getting there by error; and there were many instances where mines and explosives were discovered. And most often the regular police when they would discover something like that would inform the military police so that hundreds and hundreds of tons - and I know exactly what I'm saying, I'm very aware of my words - so we found hundreds and hundreds of tons of mines, shells, huge amounts of ammunition, guns, weapons. There was barely a house that didn't contain ammunition and weapons and so on. So this is why one of the reasons why we did not conduct many investigations into these burnings of houses because there was a fear that there were some mines planted in the house, and we were especially afraid of the mine fields because we didn't know where they were. We had losses in this area, both in civilian casualties and military casualties, and I recall this particular day when I was in Knin, one of our special officers, special policemen was killed, and his father, the man -- the boy had returned from the front line. He had brought with him a hand-grenade, and the hand-grenade went off, and he got killed and so on and so on. I have to say one more thing here. As I already mentioned, there were some 12.000 house, Croat houses that had been burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this what you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was trying to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I do want to you answer what you were about to say. There were 12.000 Croat houses that were burned. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the villages. I was born in a village between Benkovac and Knin. I lived there until my 14th year, and I know some of these villages, and I know by their names whether they were Croat or Serb villages and which villages Croats had been expelled from. I just wanted to stress this: We did not carry -- we did not conduct investigations into these Croat houses because an investigation into an arson, an instance of arson would take at least one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you didn't investigate the houses, the Croat houses that had been burned down during the 4-year occupation? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't -- I wasn't there for four years. I only spent a year and a half on those tasks. But, no, we did not investigate those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is, once the area was liberated, you didn't conduct investigations of the Croat houses that had been burned down prior to Operation Storm, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not conduct investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How -- where does this number of 12.000 Croat houses come from?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you an approximation of the villages where most such houses were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. Did you --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my free assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned the POW centres, and I would like to put certain matters to you in order to get your response. The Prosecution is making certain allegations about those centres, and I'd like to read them to you and get your response to them. In paragraph 43 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, it says: "In the centres, they", meaning the Serbs who were in the centres, "became even more aware of the systematic abuse of Serbs." The first question is, did the Croatian authorities who were running the centre purposely tell Serbs or try to instill fear in the Serbs who were in the centres?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We're first of all referring to those who were running the centre. Of course, that could include this witness, but it seems to exclude him. And now we're asking about their purpose in doing something hypothetical that they may or may not have done. I don't think he can speak to their purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we will see what his answer is, if he says, I can't say anything, or he says, I can only tell you about this, or I could -- I heard from colleagues about all the centres. We do not know. I think there is nothing inadmissible as far as the question is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regarding these centres, I stress once again that I'm proud of the way they were run - the centre in Zadar, at least - and that the citizens of the Republic of Croatia of Serb ethnicity who had been brought there because of incriminating offences that they had committed during the occupation of these areas of Croatia, they could see for themselves that we were trying to proceed as a legal state. And as far as I know, no one was killed in those centres. No one was tortured. They were given medical assistance, and some of them didn't even enter the centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the question. Mr. Misetic, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The specific question is, with respect to the centre in Zadar, did you ever see anyone trying to instill fear into the people who were in the centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Next allegation is at paragraph 115 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, and in it the Prosecution contends that: "The Serb civilians were brought to collection centres, and from these collection centres civilians were systematically transferred out of Croatia." Now, was it your experience with respect to the civilian and POW facilities in Zadar that the Croatian authorities were systematically transferring people from those centres and out of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the reception centre for prisoners of war, I claim with full awareness of what I'm saying that not a single person was transferred outside of Croatia. They were under the police jurisdiction, and there was an order of 5 August that civilian individuals can be taken over, and this referred to all -- to all adults who had their papers. They just needed to provide their information, but I don't know of any instances of anyone being transferred to one outside of Croatia. As for the centres, what I said about the centres, I claim this with full responsibility because I have direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect -- you mentioned the order of the 5th of August for -- in the civilian centre that they could leave if they had their papers and if someone came for them. What would happen in the instance of somebody who didn't have a relative, a friend, somebody who would show up and assist them in leaving the centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could leave the centre without any impediment unless the person was obviously unable to take care of themselves. Such individuals were placed in hospitals or other medical institutions, and when I say we would send them to these institutions, I mean the Croatian authorities. And in the end, when the schools were supposed to reopen on the 1st of September, a number of individuals remained there. Most of them were elderly and bedridden individuals, and they were hospitalised in a wing of the Knin hospital. This was a new hospital buildings that had been built, and this is where these persons were hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally on this topic, paragraph 125 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. This is a question about the reception centre in Knin. The allegation is that Serb civilians and surrendered RSK soldiers were detained in Croatian barracks and collection centres where they were regularly beaten and forced to work. Now, you're the chief of investigations for Zadar-Knin police administration. Did you ever receive reports of civilians in collection centres being beaten or forced to work?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. That is something that someone invented. I was in Knin. I visited the collection centre there -- the reception centre. They were not detained there, neither the civilians nor the soldiers. They were just brought there. We could not detain anyone. I've already said this. The police could not detain anyone. They could only take someone in. The courts would detain people. God forbid that we would ever try to force someone to labour, to work, either civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'd like to ask you about two deaths that are in the Prosecution's further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first one is if we could call up P251, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, this is an incident report filed by UNCIVPOL regarding the discovery of the body of Gojko Komazec. Did you participate in the investigation of the death of Gojko Komazec?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to stress that I had friendly ties indirectly with this man, although I didn't know him. He was the uncle of a well-known Croat basketball player, Arijan Komazec, and chance would have it that I knew his uncle, Milan Komazec, who lived in Zadar. He was the father of this basketball player, Arijan. And at some point in time, Milan came to me and he said that he thought his brother was in this area, so then I asked the commander of the police station in Gracac to inform me of any -- anything he knew about a person named Gojko Komazec. He told me that they had no information. In the month of March 1996, the Croatian police discovered a dead body on which documents were found bearing the name of Gojko Komazec in a place called Vevudic [phoen], not far from Zrmanja, which is the border area between Knin and Gracac. And on this occasion, the investigating judge, a pathologist, and the district attorney were called. If I recall, the pathologist determined that some bones were broken on this body and this was probably caused by a fall from a high place. This individual was then buried in the Zadar cemetery, a number was assigned to this grave, and his -- the brother of Gojko Komazec knew of this. He was aware of this. Now, there was another man called Gojko Komazec who was born the same year in the same place, but these are two different individuals. One of them is the father of Jovan - this is the dead man - and the other one was another person whose son's was Uras.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The son of Uras, interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second incident is, there was a witness who came to the Trial Chamber whose last name was Sovilj who talked about his -- members of his family that had been killed in the Gracac area. Did you participate in the investigation of the murders of members of the Sovilj family?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We processed this case in 2001 or 2002, and we were very careful. We paid a lot of attention to this investigation. A whole team of men from my section was involved in this, including me personally, because we were informed through a policeman who is a member of our staff about a possible perpetrator or a probable perpetrator of this murder. He told our policeman a story about a Croat soldier of Serb ethnicity who murdered this man immediately in the wake of Operation Storm because of some property issues that they had, and we paid a lot of attention to this investigation. We find a lot of consistencies in their stories -- in his story. There were two members of this family, Sovilj Mira --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not catch the other name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpreted] -- and they were buried in the graveyard there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We searched this home thoroughly, and we found body parts, charred body parts. We think that they were body parts because it was just a small pile of charred leftovers, and we sent this to a forensic lab for them to determine whether these were human remains or not. We investigated this, whether the perpetrator was this Croat soldier of Serb ethnicity, but so far we haven't been able to establish whether he was the perpetrator of this criminal --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, how much -- do I have any time left? I have one topic left. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was listening to the French channel, so I missed your last words. I see in the transcript only "Previous translation continues."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I don't know what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do I have any time left? I have one topic left, less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's really less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is, and I'll stop if it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And 4 minutes, 58 seconds is not less than five minutes. That's approximately three minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have P918, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a warning that you were shown yesterday by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could get the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a few questions and then show you another document. But in it, do you have any familiarity with how the Ministry of Defence works? For example, do you note that this order does not go through the military chain of command but it goes through the political line? Do you have any knowledge of how the military functioned at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Ministry of Defence has operating within it the Main Staff of the Croatian army. The chief of the staff also commands the Croatian army on behalf of the president of the state, whereas the ministry is to provide the logistical, legal, and other support to the armed forces, namely everything which comes under the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, in light of the time ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 2052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report, the next day from the chief of the political affairs unit or from an assistant in the political affairs department to the chief of the political affairs unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And here it talks about the measures that were taken by the political affairs branch to prevent crime before Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Both before and after combat operations, we made the maximum effort to indicate to members through the service the importance of exemplary and dignified entries into towns." Goes on to say: "They endeavour to prevent unnecessary devastation of religious, cultural, commercial, and civilian buildings. In cooperation with SIS and the military police, many attempts were prevented. Despite the measures taken, a certain number of civilian and commercial buildings were destroyed either in part or completely."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn -- go to the bottom of the page and then turn the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is four minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The number of such negative instances could have been reduced with better and more coordinated work between the civilian and military police and all structures of civilian and military government." My question to you, Mr. Kardum, is that was your experience as well, was it not? There was a lack of coordination between the civilian and military branches that in addition to the problems that we talked about at the beginning of my examination also contributed to the inability to establish law and order quickly. Is that correct? And I need a short answer.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to corroborate this statement is the fact that cities such as Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac were completely, almost completely preserved. I was in Knin on the 7th of August, and Knin was 90 per cent intact. Nothing had been devastated except the Catholic church of St. Anthony, which -- the roof of which had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems not to be the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I have this exhibit marked, Your Honour? I tender it into evidence, and I'm complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D810 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you're still in a position that you have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, a number of issues have arisen, so if I could deal with them as quickly as possible, I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I have a few further questions for you arising from some of the answers that you've given to Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Misetic. The first matter that I'd like to discuss is notification of complaints of crimes from international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have 65 ter 5486 displayed, and as that comes up on the screen I'll just explain. This is not a document that's on our 65 ter list. It is a cover letter that was disclosed in July 2007. The document that it encloses has been the subject of -- is on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you could look at that document there and confirm that that's your signature there and you've directed this to the sector of criminal police in Zagreb. Would that have been directed to Mr. Nadj?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature here, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And would have this letter been directed to Mr. Nadj?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The crime police sector as it is written here, to Mr. Nadj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you the enclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could please present 65 ter 4623. And if you could just go to the top of the Croatian, as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see, Mr. Kardum, that there's your -- the facsimile number of the criminal department and your name there and that it's from the commander of Knin UNCIVPOL to the commander of the Knin police station. And if we just look at a couple of examples, for instance, the first example there. We have information about someone being captured by Croatian soldiers. The second example is information about people being killed by Croatian soldiers. Do you recall receiving that and forwarding it on to Mr. Nadj in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just go through it a bit, please? Yes, I see this text, and I can see my first and last names written up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And can you confirm that you forwarded that to Mr. Nadj in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is evident from the first section if that is a component part of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if could I have the cover letter entered into evidence and together with this appendix to that cover letter, so that's 65 ter 5486 and 65 ter 46 -- 623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to the admission, but I think the purpose of the document should be put to the witness as to why -- what the purpose is and why it's being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. No contest from me. I do have another document which is of a similar nature which I'd like to show the witness and put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it seems that Mr. Margetts wants to establish that this document was sent by the witness to Zagreb, and if he has any further questions, we'll hear from him or, as a matter of fact, the witness will hear from him. Mr. Margetts, then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05486, that becomes Exhibit number P921; and 65 ter 04623 becomes Exhibit number P922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P921 and P922 are admitted into evidence. I don't know whether it's very practical to have it under two numbers, but for the time being we leave it as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have document identification 1D54-0033 produced on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is the same objection that's now the subject of a pending motion, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, and Your Honour, this is a cover page which -- as Mr. Misetic indicates that we've received from the Defence, and it -- the enclosure is D179 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But if, Mr. Kardum, you could please look at this document, and could you confirm that, again, this is it a letter that you send to Mr. Nadj; and could you please just have a look at the second paragraph and confirm that you asked Mr. Nadj for further instructions as to how to proceed?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. So, Mr. Kardum, can you confirm that you in fact did receive complaints from internationals in relation to crimes that had occurred on the territory?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please see the second page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, does this move to a second page? It did -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that this document was sent to Ivica Cetina and not to Ivo Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You can confirm, however, that you did receive this and this is a list of complaints from internationals?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was received by the police administration by the chief Ivan Cetina. After talking about it, we forwarded it to the ministry, and that was after the date which this document bears, which is the 27th of September. Immediately after that date, we had this great project that we embarked upon to process various crimes. I actually asked the head for his instructions, meaning to ask for assistance. So he arrived and the Assistant Minister Benko and with an entire entourage of police officers who came to conduct this procedure about all these murders that were referred to in the document. But I do have an objection to raise in respect of the representatives of the international community because they informed us about crimes that have happened on 4th or 5th of August on the 27th. I wonder why did they not inform us immediately because I believe that there are also some falsehoods in the text, and it is a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they got by their information. One of the persons referred to is Gojko Komazec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have this marked for identification in light of Mr. Misetic's reservations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the English and the Croatian copies on our screen at this moment. They are of different dates, the one 23rd of September, 1995; the other one of the 19th September, 1995. Now, it may well be that in the routine at that time that two versions were not produced exactly at the same time, but could we look again at the previous one where apparently this witness writes a letter and forwards the ... because I'd like to look at the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There, at least I didn't see that, that at least there's specific reference made to a document submitted in a language on a certain date, apparently not yet in B/C/S at that moment. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object on the basis of the motion that's currently pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's because of the disclosure of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's not on the 65 ter list as part of the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. So apart from that objection, there are no other objections. Then we'll deal with that matter. I'll discuss with my colleagues how to deal with it, either to have them marked for identification. I think we admitted the previous document where there was a similar objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first one that I presented today was just one that we -- had become relevant and I sought to add to the 65 ter list, but it emanated from the Prosecution, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you earlier referred to a pending motion and objection based on that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that motion has many or multiple components, one of which is that these documents are not on the 65 ter list, but there's also an Article 21 argument in the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further analyse what decisions on admission were taken earlier and see whether we have to review those decisions in light of the pending motion for this document. At least at this moment, it will be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, that would be number...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P923 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, at the start of your examination by Mr. Misetic, he indicated the change in the geographic area that the police were responsible for after Operation Storm, and I'd just like you to indicate, was it the case that in that additional area, the Knin area and surrounds, there was a very great change in demographics during and immediately after Operation Storm; that is, did a lot of people depart from at that territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this an issue in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The issue being I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I do understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you want to inform the Chamber of the fact that if there's less population, there's less work to be done, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the fact you're seeking to establish seems to be not in dispute. Please make a clear distinction between what you could argue at a later stage and whether this is any fact that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's argumentative at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in early August 1995, Mr. Kardum, there were many military personnel on the territory, the newly acquired territory or liberated territory under your police administration, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Many" is a relative concept. There were soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have D49 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'm going to show you again the 18 August order from Mr. Moric, and we dealt with that in the course of the examination. In particular, we dealt with paragraph 5. In this order, there's a reference by Mr. Moric, and if we could just stay on that first page there, please, Mr. Registrar, for a moment. There's a reference for Mr. Moric that you will see there, Mr. Kardum, to the fact that there were many acts perpetrated by individuals wearing Croatian army uniforms. And if we can please turn over now to paragraph 5, you will see that, again, this is the paragraph we looked at a day or so ago. It says if the military police cannot perform the tasks, then the police will do it, irrespective of whether the perpetrator wears a Croatian army uniform. Now, at that stage, what was your practice in relation to these incidents where the perpetrator was wearing a Croatian army uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could establish what time-period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The time-period, Mr. Kardum, indicated in this correspondence, the correspondence is 18 August. So in the period from the 5th of August to 18 August, and if there is a distinction, please make it, but I'm also interested in the remainder of August.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter by Mr. Moric was sent by Mr. Moric, the assistant minister of the regular police, to the chief of the police administration. I'm not quite sure whether and when I received this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- the question is not when you received it but what your practice was at that time, between the 5th and the 18th of August, if -- of course, in view of this instruction, whether you did act alone irrespective of whether the perpetrator wore a Croatian army uniform or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The practice was as I described it before. Namely, we would detain them until the military police came. We would process them if there was no military police, and then we would subsequently inform the military police thereon, and I have described this several times, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the practice change after the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in particular, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that you described the practice also before the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You were also asked about the process of sanitation, and I'd just like to confirm with you that there were -- there was a distinct responsibility for sanitation that -- that the civil protection department had, and that was a different responsibility to the responsibility of the criminal administration had for criminal investigation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any -- it seems so obvious to me that is the whole line of the way in which the witness answered all of the questions. Is there any need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There appears to be an issue that arose. If I could please have D233 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This, Mr. Kardum, may assist you. This is an order from Zdravko Zidovec, and you've seen this before. It's been referred to in your 2007 witness statement. And if you could just look at this order, you will see that Zdravko Zidovec, the assistant minister responsible for civil protection, has indicated the various tasks that will be performed in respect of the identification of bodies. And so can you please look at that and confirm that there's no reference in any part of this order to any investigative steps?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Zidovec was the assistant minister for civilian protection affairs, and what you have just stated is correct. He was not in charge of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it's the case that the forensic technicians that were assigned to the sanitation teams were assigned to teams that came under the jurisdiction of Zidovec and more immediately, Cemeron. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were under the jurisdiction of the assistant minister for the crime police. They were part of the crime police, but at that moment they were assigned to assist the civilian protection crews working on the territory, and their specific assignments are spelled out in Items 1 and 2 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And also, we had the opportunity to see the order that came from Maric on the 6th of August. And similarly, the task prescribed was one of identification, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the issue that I want to ask you directly about is this.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maric --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The role that we saw prescribed by Zidovec's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, it seems that your last question did not receive -- the answer to your last question was not interpreted. It's [Microphone not activated] appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I -- the interpreter failed to switch on her microphone. Can I repeat it? I know what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can repeat the answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the chief of all forensic technicians at the level of the MUP. He was generally the chief of all the forensic technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. That's not specifically my question. My question is, we've seen Zidovec's order, and earlier we've seen Maric's order. We also had the benefit of seeing the crime police sector minutes from the meetings that were held in Zagreb. The role of the forensic technicians was prescribed there, and it was one of identification, wasn't it? That was the role that they were given.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and that is in Item 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'm looking at the clock. How much time would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really -- I could complete the examination in the next five minutes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Defence already indicate whether the questions put until now trigger any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm hoping that Mr. Margetts will put to him what he wants to interpret this order as. If he does that, then I won't ask any questions. If he doesn't, I'm going to put it to him in one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then with the indulgence of the interpreters and everyone else who assists us, I'd like to finish, as a matter of fact, and that should be done within the next eight minutes unless this finds strong opposition. Well, I haven't -- as to the objections, I hear of no strong opposition. Thank you very much already in advance. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts, and stick to your time estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At Mr. Misetic's invitation, I'll move straight to the issue, and that is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That the forensic technicians who were assigned to the sanitation teams, they performed the task of identification of the bodies, but they didn't conduct any onsite investigation, did they?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you completely because they photographed the site -- the scene of the crime, which is part of on-site investigations, which is part of the forensic technician's job. So not completely, but in part they did perform some investigative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And those investigative actions are prescribed in the orders of Zidovec and in the order of Maric that we saw?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Maric was a lower-level officer in the criminal police. He was the subordinate to Mr. Zidovec, and I think that he even referred to this order from Mr. Zidovec. He was the chief of all forensic technicians in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one issue, and that's the exhibits that I need to tender. If we could attend to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that we'll deal with that tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not ask more from those who are assisting us. Mr. Kardum, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you for coming the far way to The Hague and for having answered the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.
